title: Channels of Distribution
summary: A channel of distribution is the route or path along which goods and services move from producers to the final consumers. The persons in between — agents, wholesalers and retailers — are middlemen (intermediaries): links between producers and consumers who buy, sell, store and distribute. Example: an apple grower in Srinagar sells to an agent, who sells to a Delhi wholesaler, who sells to retailers, from whom we buy.

Direct channel (zero-level): Producer → Consumer, with no middleman — door-to-door salesmen, the producer's own shops (Bata, Liberty), mail-order selling, online sales by the producer. It suits heavy equipment and machinery, expensive or perishable goods and most services — banking, insurance, consultancy, telephone, transport, education, medical and legal services are all delivered directly.

Indirect channels: Producer → Retailer → Consumer (one level; big retailers such as departmental stores and super bazars buy in bulk; also local goods like bread and biscuits); Producer → Wholesaler → Retailer → Consumer (two levels; most common for food grains, spices, utensils, consumer goods); Producer → Agent → Wholesaler → Retailer → Consumer (long channel); Producer → Agent → Consumer; Producer → Wholesaler → Consumer. A channel with both wholesalers and retailers is a long channel. The retailer is the last link before the consumer.

Wholesalers buy goods in bulk directly from producers and sell in smaller lots to retailers (sometimes to large consumers). Characteristics: buy in large quantities; deal in a limited range, usually one line of goods with all its varieties; need a large amount of capital; give credit to retailers and finance to producers; have no direct contact with consumers; are usually found in one area of the market; spend little on shop decoration. Functions: collection (assembling) of goods; storage in warehouses and cold storage; distribution to retailers; financing producers and retailers; risk bearing (fall in price, spoilage, change in demand); grading, packing and branding; pricing and stabilising prices by matching supply with demand; supplying market information.

Retailers buy from wholesalers (or producers) and sell in small quantities to consumers for their own use. Characteristics: direct contact with consumers; sell in small quantities for consumption, not resale; need less capital; keep a wide variety of goods; buy on credit but sell mostly for cash; pay attention to decoration and display. Functions: buying and assembling a variety of goods; storage, so consumers need not store; credit to regular customers; personal services — advice, home delivery (place utility); risk bearing — fire or theft, deterioration of goods, change in fashion and taste; display of goods; supplying information about consumers' tastes to producers through wholesalers; creating demand for new products.

Quantity — wholesaler buys and sells in bulk; retailer in small quantities. Source — wholesaler buys from producers; retailer from wholesalers. Variety — wholesaler deals in a limited line; retailer in a wide range. Capital — more for a wholesaler, less for a retailer. Purpose of sale — wholesaler sells for resale; retailer for consumption. Contact with consumers — wholesaler none; retailer direct. Decoration — little for a wholesaler; much for a retailer.

vsa: What risks are borne by retailers? Mention any two.

(1) Loss of goods by fire or theft.
(2) Deterioration in quality of goods while they remain unsold.
(3) Change in fashion and taste of consumers, leaving goods unsold. (Any two.)
A publisher sells books to a wholesaler who sells to local bookstores. Name the channel and the role of the wholesaler.

Channel: Producer (publisher) → Wholesaler → Retailer (bookstores) → Consumer — an indirect, two-level channel.
The wholesaler buys in bulk, stores the books and distributes them in smaller lots to bookstores, often on credit.

or: How do retailers help in stabilising prices?
Retailers keep stocks and buy regularly from wholesalers, so goods are available steadily; by informing wholesalers about demand they help match supply with demand, which keeps prices stable.

vsa: State any two functions of a retailer.

(1) Buying and assembling a variety of goods from many suppliers.
(2) Personal service — advice and home delivery; also credit to regular customers, display and storage of goods.

or: What is a direct channel? Give two examples.
A channel in which the producer sells directly to the consumer without any middleman. Examples: Bata selling through its own shops; banking, insurance and telephone services; door-to-door selling.

vsa:
(1) Storage — they store goods in warehouses until retailers need them.
(2) Financing — they give advances to producers and credit to retailers.
(Also: collection, distribution, risk bearing, grading, pricing.)
sa: Explain the role of retailers in the distribution of goods.

(1) They buy and assemble goods from many wholesalers and producers and make them available near consumers.
(2) They sell in small quantities, saving consumers from storing goods.
(3) They give credit, advice and home delivery.
(4) They pass on information about consumers' tastes to producers and help introduce new products.
How do retailers help consumers? Give any three ways.

(1) Regular supply of a variety of goods near the home, in small quantities.
(2) Personal service — guidance on quality and use, home delivery and credit facility.
(3) Attractive display and information about new products, helping consumers choose.

or: State any three services of wholesalers to manufacturers.

(1) Bulk buying — they buy in large quantities, so the manufacturer is spared many small orders.
(2) Storage — they keep goods in their own warehouses, relieving the manufacturer of storage.
(3) Finance and information — they often pay in cash or in advance and pass on market information about demand and tastes.

sa: What services do wholesalers provide to retailers? State any three.

(1) Ready supply — retailers can get a variety of goods from one wholesaler in small lots whenever needed.
(2) Credit facility — wholesalers often sell on credit, so retailers need less capital.
(3) Information — they tell retailers about new products, prices and market trends.
(4) Less risk of storage — retailers need not keep large stocks.
Define retailers and state any three of their functions.

Retailers are traders who buy goods from wholesalers or producers and sell them in small quantities to final consumers.
Functions: buying and assembling goods; storage; credit and personal services; risk bearing; display; supply of information.
la: What is a channel of distribution? Explain the various types of channels.

A channel of distribution is the route along which goods move from the producer to the final consumer, through middlemen if needed.
Direct channel: Producer → Consumer — through the producer's own shops, door-to-door salesmen, mail order; used for services and heavy equipment.
Indirect channels: (1) Producer → Retailer → Consumer — for big retailers and local goods; (2) Producer → Wholesaler → Retailer → Consumer — the common channel for consumer goods; (3) Producer → Agent → Wholesaler → Retailer → Consumer — long channel for goods sold over wide areas; (4) Producer → Agent → Consumer; (5) Producer → Wholesaler → Consumer.
What is meant by channels of distribution? Explain any four services distributed through the direct channel, with examples.

A channel of distribution is the path by which goods and services reach consumers from producers.
Services are produced and consumed at the same time, so they are distributed directly:
(1) Banking — the bank serves customers at its branches and online (SBI).
(2) Insurance — the company or its own agents issue policies (LIC).
(3) Transport — railways, airlines and buses carry passengers directly.
(4) Telephone and Internet services (BSNL, Airtel).
(5) Medical, legal, education and consultancy services.
Explain any five functions of retailers.

(1) Buying and assembling goods of many brands and varieties.
(2) Storage — keeping stock so consumers can buy any time.
(3) Credit facility to regular customers.
(4) Personal services — advice, after-sales help and home delivery.
(5) Risk bearing — fire, theft, spoilage, change in fashion.
(6) Display and supply of information to producers.
State any four functions of a wholesaler.

(1) Collection of goods in bulk from producers.
(2) Storage until goods are sold.
(3) Distribution to retailers.
(4) Financing producers (advances) and retailers (credit).
(5) Risk bearing, grading and packing, and stabilising prices.
State any six differences between wholesalers and retailers.

(1) Quantity — bulk vs small.
(2) Buy from — producers vs wholesalers.
(3) Variety — limited line vs wide range.
(4) Capital — more vs less.
(5) Sale — for resale vs for consumption.
(6) Contact with consumers — none vs direct.
(7) Decoration of shop — little vs much.
